set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea also has heart failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She asks for the adjustable device a friend uses. Which device should she not be given?
opts: Correct. Autotitrating (adjustable) positive airway pressure is used in patients without significant comorbid conditions. Her heart failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are significant comorbidities, so she should get continuous positive airway pressure, the most effective option, instead.

Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective treatment, and no comorbidity limit is attached to it. Tell: it is the device she should receive; the comorbidity limit belongs to the autotitrating device.

A nasal expiratory resistance device uses the patient's own breathing to produce expiratory positive airway pressure, and no comorbidity limit is attached to it. Tell: the device kept for patients without significant comorbidities is the autotitrating one.

An oral appliance is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea or in patients with no teeth, and neither applies to her. Tell: her heart failure and lung disease restrict the autotitrating device, not the appliance.

set1.q: A 45-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has a body mass index of 36 kg/m2. He asks what he can do himself, in addition to using his positive airway pressure device. Which risk modification fits him?
opts: Sleeping on his back each night

Positional therapy keeps the patient on his side, with a sleep belt or sleep shirt, when events occur while supine. Tell: lying on his back is the position the therapy avoids; for his obesity the self-care step is weight loss.
A nightly sedative to deepen sleep

Sedatives are a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the advice is to avoid them. Tell: a sedative works against him; diet and exercise for weight loss is the change that addresses his body mass index of 36.
An evening glass of wine to relax
Alcohol is a risk factor, and avoiding alcohol and other sedatives is a named risk modification. Tell: relaxing with wine works against him; diet and exercise for weight loss target his obesity.
Diet and exercise for weight loss

Correct. Obesity heads the risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea, and diet and exercise for weight loss is a named risk modification, together with avoiding alcohol and other sedatives. Bariatric surgery for weight loss may also be helpful.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man has habitual snoring and daytime sleepiness. During 6 hours of sleep his polysomnogram records 48 apneas, 42 hypopneas and 36 respiratory effort-related arousals, predominantly obstructive. What is his apnea-hypopnea index?
opts: 7 is the hypopneas alone, 42 / 6, leaving out his 48 apneas. Tell: the index adds apneas and hypopneas before dividing by the hours of sleep, so (48 + 42) / 6 = 15 events per hour.
8 is the apneas alone, 48 / 6, leaving out his 42 hypopneas. Tell: both event types are counted in the numerator, (48 + 42) / 6 = 15, and only the arousals stay out.

Correct. The apnea-hypopnea index is (apneas + hypopneas) divided by total sleep time in hours: (48 + 42) / 6 = 90 / 6 = 15 events per hour. Respiratory effort-related arousals belong to the respiratory disturbance index, not to this one. At 15 or more predominantly obstructive events, the diagnosis is confirmed.
21 adds the 36 respiratory effort-related arousals: (48 + 42 + 36) / 6 = 21, which is his respiratory disturbance index. Tell: the apnea-hypopnea index leaves the arousals out and comes to 15.

set1.q: A 53-year-old man has loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness, and his primary care clinician suspects obstructive sleep apnea. Which referral is part of his care?
opts: Maxillomandibular advancement is one of many surgical options for established disease. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, and the referral named in patient education is to a sleep physician.

Untreated obstructive sleep apnea raises cardiovascular risks such as hypertension, arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death at night, but the referral named for the sleep disorder is a sleep physician. Tell: he is being evaluated for the apnea itself.

Correct. Patient education for obstructive sleep apnea includes referral to a sleep physician, together with proper counseling. His snoring, witnessed apneas and sleepiness make the diagnosis likely, and confirming it takes a sleep study.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it is a surgical option rather than the referral named for a suspected diagnosis. Tell: the named referral is to a sleep physician, with proper counseling.

set1.q: A 43-year-old woman with habitual snoring and daytime sleepiness has a home sleep apnea test that does not show obstructive sleep apnea. Her symptoms persist. What is the best next step?
opts: A negative home study does not exclude mild disease, since home kits will not always diagnose it. Tell: her symptoms persist, so the question stays open until a polysomnogram answers it.

Repeating the same kind of study repeats its limits: home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea alone and can miss mild disease. Tell: the polysomnogram is the study that measures severity across sleep stages and positions.

Stimulants such as modafinil treat sleepiness but carry headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and treating the symptom would skip the study that could find mild disease.

Correct. At-home kits will not always diagnose mild obstructive sleep apnea; they are most helpful in moderate to severe disease. A negative home study in a woman with ongoing snoring and sleepiness therefore needs a polysomnogram, which can also find other sleep disorders a home kit cannot assess.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man with heart failure has insomnia and frequent awakenings, and central sleep apnea is suspected. Which study establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Central sleep apnea is diagnosed by polysomnography, and at-home testing is not sufficient. The study shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion, and heart failure is also a reason to use a polysomnogram rather than a home kit.

At-home testing is not sufficient for central sleep apnea; home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders. Tell: his heart failure adds a second reason for an in-laboratory study.
ruled out by a stated finding

An arterial blood gas measures awake carbon dioxide, the test that follows a serum bicarbonate above 27 when obesity hypoventilation syndrome is suspected. Tell: central apnea is a pattern of events during sleep, shown on polysomnography.

A thyroid-stimulating hormone level is added to a sleep evaluation when hypothyroidism is suspected. Tell: it cannot show apneas; repetitive apneas without thoracic-abdominal excursion are seen on polysomnography.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman has severe obstructive sleep apnea on polysomnogram. She finds her mask uncomfortable and asks whether an oral appliance would work as well. What should she be told?
opts: It works if she sleeps on her back
Sleeping supine is the position positional therapy avoids, keeping the patient on her side when events occur supine. Tell: no sleeping position makes an appliance effective in severe disease.
It equals the mask if worn nightly
Nightly use does not change the limit: the appliance is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her severity, not how often she would wear it, rules the appliance out.
It is not effective in severe disease

Correct. An oral appliance is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea or in patients without teeth. Her disease is severe, so the appliance is not a substitute; continuous positive airway pressure remains the most effective treatment for her.
It is the most effective option
Continuous positive airway pressure is the option named most effective, not the oral appliance. Tell: for her severe disease the appliance is not effective at all, so it cannot match the mask.

set1.q: A 56-year-old woman with a body mass index of 44 kg/m2 has daytime hypersomnolence, loud snoring and dyspnea on exertion. Awake on room air, her arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 54 mm Hg (normal 35-45). Her chest radiograph, thyroid function tests, pulmonary function tests and toxicology screen show no other cause of hypoventilation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Her snoring and hypersomnolence fit obstructive sleep apnea, which coexists in about 90% of these patients, but it does not account for awake hypercapnia of 54 mm Hg. Tell: awake carbon dioxide above 45 in an obese patient, other causes excluded, defines obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Central sleep apnea is a pattern of apneas without respiratory effort during sleep, tied to heart failure, stroke, opioids or altitude. Tell: she has none of those, and her defining finding is awake hypercapnia with obesity.

Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness. Tell: it does not explain an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, which with a body mass index above 30 points to obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion made when obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake alveolar hypoventilation (arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg) are present and alternative causes of hypercapnia are excluded. Her 44 kg/m2, 54 mm Hg and negative workup meet all three.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea declines treatment and asks how the condition affects his heart. Which risk is raised 3 to 6 times in untreated disease?
opts: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea triples the risk of hypertension (3 times). Tell: the 3- to 6-fold figure belongs to sudden cardiac death, and specifically to death at night.

Driving accidents are 2.5 times more frequent in untreated disease, because daytime sleepiness increases motor vehicle crashes. Tell: that figure is lower and is not a heart risk; 3 to 6 times is sudden cardiac death at night.

Correct. Untreated obstructive sleep apnea carries a 3- to 6-fold risk of sudden cardiac death at night, alongside high mortality from heart failure. The timing is the point: the excess risk falls during sleep, when the apneas occur.
The excess risk of sudden cardiac death in untreated disease is at night, during sleep, not with exertion. Tell: the 3- to 6-fold figure is tied to nighttime, when the obstructive events happen.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea drinks several glasses of wine each night and takes an over-the-counter sedative to fall asleep. Which advice addresses these modifiable risk factors?
opts: Correct. Use of alcohol or sedatives is a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the risk modifications are to avoid alcohol and other sedatives, along with diet and exercise for weight loss. Both his nightly wine and his sleep aid fall under that advice.
Keep the sedative, stop the wine

Stopping the wine while keeping the sedative leaves one of the two named risk factors in place. Tell: the advice covers alcohol and other sedatives together, so the over-the-counter sleep aid has to go as well as the wine.
Keep the wine, stop the sedative

Stopping the sedative while keeping the wine leaves alcohol, itself a listed risk factor, in his nightly routine. Tell: risk modification names alcohol together with other sedatives, so the wine is part of the problem too.
Take both earlier in the evening

Changing the timing still leaves alcohol and a sedative in his routine, and the risk modification is to avoid them. Tell: the advice is avoidance of alcohol and other sedatives, not rescheduling them around bedtime.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with a body mass index of 41 kg/m2 has loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. His awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 49 mm Hg (normal 35-45). Which sleep study should be avoided in his evaluation?
opts: Correct. In patients with awake hypoventilation a polysomnogram is used, not an at-home kit, and home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea without other sleep disorders. His awake carbon dioxide of 49 mm Hg is awake hypoventilation, and the gold standard for suspected obesity hypoventilation is polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.

Polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring is the gold standard for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Tell: it is the study he should have; the one set aside in awake hypoventilation is the home kit.
An in-laboratory polysomnogram is the study used when awake hypoventilation is present. Tell: it is recommended for him; the kit is the study to avoid.
A positive airway pressure titration sets the device pressure once the diagnosis is known, a legitimate later step. Tell: the study set aside in awake hypoventilation is the at-home kit.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnea cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure despite several mask changes. Which option is described for his severity and his intolerance of the device?
opts: Palatal implants are used in mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: his disease is moderate, beyond the mild range the implants cover; radiofrequency ablation reaches mild to moderate.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered for central sleep apnea after continuous positive airway pressure fails, and it is itself a positive airway pressure therapy. Tell: his disease is obstructive, and his problem is tolerating pressure therapy.

Modafinil is a stimulant for sleepiness, with headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: no severity or device-intolerance indication is attached to it; radiofrequency ablation carries exactly his two.

Correct. Radiofrequency ablation is used in patients with mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. His disease is moderate and he cannot tolerate the device, which matches both conditions.

set1.q: A 60-year-old man with long-standing untreated obstructive sleep apnea declines therapy. Which cardiovascular effect is expected from his untreated disease?
opts: Correct. The cardiovascular effects of untreated obstructive sleep apnea include increased sympathetic tone, bradycardia, increased blood pressure variability, increased arrhythmias and an increased risk of aortic aneurysms and aortic dissections.

Blood pressure variability increases in untreated obstructive sleep apnea; it does not fall. Tell: the listed cardiovascular increases are sympathetic tone, blood pressure variability, arrhythmias and the risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection.

Sympathetic tone is increased in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, not reduced. Tell: the cardiovascular list pairs increased sympathetic tone with more blood pressure variability, more arrhythmias and more aortic dissection risk.

Arrhythmias increase in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, alongside a 3- to 6-fold risk of sudden cardiac death at night. Tell: untreated disease adds rhythm problems rather than protecting against them.

set1.q: A 52-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated events in which thermistor airflow falls by 90% or more for 15 seconds while chest and abdominal respiratory effort continue. How is each event classified?
opts: A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, short of a near-total stop. Tell: a fall in airflow of 90% or more is near or total cessation of breathing, which defines an apnea.

Correct. An apnea is a 90% or greater fall in airflow on the thermistor lasting at least 10 seconds, and when airflow stops but respiratory effort continues, the apnea is obstructive. The airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe, the event pattern of obstructive sleep apnea.

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops sending the signal to breathe. Tell: his chest and abdomen keep moving throughout each event, so effort is present and the event is not central.
ruled out by a stated finding

A mixed apnea opens with no respiratory effort, and effort resumes only during the latter part of the event. Tell: his effort is present from the start of each event to its end, which is the obstructive pattern rather than the mixed one.

set1.q: A 48-year-old woman with newly diagnosed obesity hypoventilation syndrome asks to start a weight-loss medication instead of a diet and exercise program. What should she be told?
opts: Medication follows failed diet and exercise

Correct. Medications for obesity hypoventilation syndrome are reserved for those who fail diet and exercise measures. First line is a weight loss program with lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, behavioral modification) plus positive airway pressure, within a multidisciplinary approach.
First line is a weight loss program plus bilevel or continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: medications are second line, used for those who fail diet and exercise measures.
Positive airway pressure is part of first-line therapy along with weight loss, and medication is not offered as its substitute. Tell: drugs enter the plan later, after diet and exercise fail.

Bariatric surgery and medications both appear among the second-line options for patients who fail first-line therapy. Tell: the condition attached to medication is failure of diet and exercise, not prior surgery.

set1.q: A 41-year-old woman has daytime sleepiness, and her partner reports habitual snoring and pauses in her breathing. Her polysomnogram shows 8 predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour, and her symptoms are not explained by another condition, a medication or a substance. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed with 5 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour plus a symptom such as sleepiness, or habitual snoring and breathing interruptions noted by a bed partner, when no other condition, medication or substance explains them. She has 8 events and those symptoms.
Not diagnostic until 15 events per hour
15 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour confirm the diagnosis without any symptom. Tell: she has symptoms, so the lower threshold of 5 events per hour applies, and her 8 events meet it.

Central sleep apnea shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion, airflow stopping because effort stops. Tell: her events are predominantly obstructive, the defining feature of obstructive sleep apnea.
Indeterminate until a home kit is done

A home kit will not always diagnose mild disease and adds nothing after a polysomnogram has answered the question. Tell: her result already meets the criterion of 5 or more events per hour with symptoms.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman with loud snoring and fatigue has an 8-hour polysomnogram that records 40 apneas, 32 hypopneas and 40 respiratory effort-related arousals. What is her respiratory disturbance index?
opts: 4 is the hypopneas alone, 32 / 8. Tell: the respiratory disturbance index counts apneas, hypopneas and respiratory effort-related arousals together, which gives 112 / 8 = 14.
5 is a single event type over the night, 40 / 8, either the apneas or the arousals. Tell: this index sums all three event types before dividing by the 8 hours of sleep, giving 14.
9 is the apnea-hypopnea index, (40 + 32) / 8, which leaves out the arousals. Tell: the respiratory disturbance index adds the 40 respiratory effort-related arousals, (40 + 32 + 40) / 8 = 14.

Correct. The respiratory disturbance index is (apneas + hypopneas + respiratory effort-related arousals) divided by total sleep time in hours: (40 + 32 + 40) / 8 = 112 / 8 = 14 events per hour. The arousals are obstructive airflow reductions that are neither apneas nor hypopneas.

set1.q: A 50-year-old man started modafinil for residual daytime sleepiness from obstructive sleep apnea. Two weeks later he develops a widespread rash and feels unwell. Which adverse effect of the drug best fits?
opts: Worsening sleep apnea would bring more sleepiness, snoring or witnessed apneas, the features of the disease. Tell: a new rash after a new drug points to the drug's listed dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivities.
Headache is a listed side effect of modafinil, but it does not produce a rash. Tell: skin involvement with feeling unwell is the hypersensitivity pattern, a separate listed side effect.

Correct. Listed side effects of modafinil and armodafinil include headaches, nervousness or anxiety, dizziness, nausea, and dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivities. A widespread rash with feeling unwell after starting the drug fits a dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivity reaction.

Nervousness and anxiety are listed side effects, but they are feelings, not a skin eruption. Tell: a widespread rash with systemic illness matches the dermatologic and systemic hypersensitivities listed for the stimulants.

set1.q: A 50-year-old woman with a body mass index of 41 kg/m2 and obstructive sleep apnea is being evaluated, and her clinician's suspicion of obesity hypoventilation syndrome is low to moderate. Her serum bicarbonate is 31 mEq/L (normal 22-29). What is the next step?
opts: Repeating the bicarbonate delays the step its result already triggers: above 27, the chance of the syndrome is higher and an arterial blood gas is needed. Tell: her 31 mEq/L is already above 27.

A home kit assesses obstructive sleep apnea, which she already has, and is set aside when awake hypoventilation is a concern. Tell: the missing measurement is her awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure, which comes from a blood gas.

A raised bicarbonate is a screening clue, not a criterion; the diagnosis needs an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg and exclusion of other causes. Tell: the bicarbonate decides who gets the blood gas.

Correct. When suspicion is low to moderate, a serum bicarbonate above 27 means a higher chance of obesity hypoventilation syndrome and the need for an arterial blood gas. Her 31 mEq/L crosses that line, and the gas measures the awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure the diagnosis requires (above 45 mm Hg).

set1.io: Discuss screening tools for obstructive sleep apnea
set1.q: A 42-year-old woman snores loudly and is treated for high blood pressure. She denies daytime tiredness, and no one has seen her stop breathing. Her body mass index is 32 kg/m2 and her neck (shirt collar) measures 16 inches. Using the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire, which result fits her?
opts: A score of 2 misses the neck item: the questionnaire counts a collar of 16 inches / 40 cm or larger, and hers is 16 inches. Tell: with the neck counted she has 3, and the neck with 2 yes answers to the first 4 questions makes her high risk.

The total of 3 is right, but 2 or more yes answers to the first 4 questions plus a neck of 16 inches / 40 cm is a separate high-risk rule. Tell: the 3-to-4 band holds only when no add-on rule is met, and her neck meets one.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed 0 + treated pressure 1 + body mass index 32 (not above 35) 0 + age 42 0 + neck 16 inches 1 + female 0 = 3. By count that is intermediate, but yes to 2 or more of the first 4 questions plus a neck of 16 inches / 40 cm is a high-risk rule, so she is high risk.

A score of 4 counts her body mass index, but the B item asks for more than 35 kg/m2, and 32 does not qualify. Tell: her total is 3; she reaches high risk through the neck rule, not through a higher count.

ruled out by a stated finding

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort for the whole event. Tell: effort comes back during the latter part of each of her events, so the event does not stay central from start to finish.
ruled out by a stated finding

A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, with airflow reduced rather than absent. Tell: her airflow is absent, so these are apneas, and the effort pattern makes them mixed.

Correct. A mixed apnea has no airflow, with a lack of respiratory effort during the first part of the event and resumption of effort during the latter part. Her events begin like central apneas and end like obstructive ones, which is exactly the mixed pattern.

opts: Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it sits in second line, after first-line therapy fails or is not tolerated. Tell: first line is a weight loss program plus positive airway pressure.
Weight loss plus bilevel positive airway pressure

Correct. First-line therapy for obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a weight loss program with positive airway pressure, and the device follows the overlap: with sleep-related hypoventilation it is bilevel positive airway pressure. Her few witnessed apneas, older age and female sex fit that 10% subgroup.
Weight loss plus continuous positive airway pressure

Continuous positive airway pressure is the first-line device when obesity hypoventilation coexists with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her study shows sleep-related hypoventilation with few witnessed apneas, which calls for bilevel pressure.

Correct. Treatment of central sleep apnea addresses an underlying cause (heart failure, opioids or altitude), and none applies to her. The next step is to consider continuous positive airway pressure first, with adaptive servo-ventilation held for when it fails.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered if continuous positive airway pressure fails, and it is not used for every patient because of safety concerns. Tell: she has not yet tried continuous pressure.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is the first-line device, with weight loss, for obesity hypoventilation syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation. Tell: for central sleep apnea, the device considered first is continuous positive airway pressure.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with heart failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness. His insurer suggests a home sleep apnea kit. Which test should be used instead?
opts: A thyroid-stimulating hormone level is added when hypothyroidism is suspected, and it does not diagnose a sleep disorder. Tell: nothing here suggests thyroid disease; the question is which sleep study his heart and lung disease allow.

Correct. At-home kits suit uncomplicated suspected obstructive sleep apnea, but in significant cardiopulmonary disease a polysomnogram is used, not an at-home kit. His heart failure and chronic lung disease are that comorbidity, and heart failure is also a risk factor for central apnea, which a home kit cannot assess.
Home sleep apnea kit at a later date

Delaying the same study does not remove the problem: at-home kits are set aside in significant cardiopulmonary disease. Tell: his heart failure and lung disease, not the timing, decide that he needs a polysomnogram.
ruled out by a stated finding

A positive airway pressure titration study is used when the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing is already known, to set the pressure. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, so the first study has to establish one.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has not been helped by continuous positive airway pressure or an oral appliance. He asks which operation would be a cure. Which procedure is described as a cure for obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Palatal implants are an option in mild obstructive sleep apnea for patients who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: they treat mild disease; the cure comes from bypassing the upper airway obstruction.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate disease when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: it is a treatment option; tracheostomy, which bypasses the obstruction, is the one called a cure.

Correct. Tracheostomy is a cure for obstructive sleep apnea because the site of upper airway obstruction is bypassed. Breathing no longer depends on the narrowed upper airway that collapses during sleep.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful in obstructive sleep apnea, a weaker claim than a cure. Tell: the procedure called a cure is the one that bypasses the site of obstruction, tracheostomy.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and central sleep apnea. His heart failure therapy has been optimized, and continuous positive airway pressure has failed. Which therapy should be avoided because of his heart failure?
opts: Polysomnography is how central sleep apnea is diagnosed, and no heart failure restriction is attached to it. Tell: the hazard in reduced ejection fraction is the preload-lowering effect of adaptive servo-ventilation.

Correct. Adaptive servo-ventilation is the usual step after continuous positive airway pressure fails, but it is not used for every patient, especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: with poor left ventricular function, reducing preload can decrease cardiac output. Cheyne-Stokes breathing can also be protective.

Continuous positive airway pressure is considered first in central sleep apnea, and no reduced-ejection-fraction warning is attached to it. Tell: the safety warning tied to poor left ventricular function belongs to adaptive servo-ventilation.

Optimizing heart failure therapy is the cause-directed treatment of central apnea in heart failure, and it is recommended, not avoided. Tell: the therapy that can lower his cardiac output by reducing preload is adaptive servo-ventilation.

opts: A titration study sets the device pressure once the diagnosis is known. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and her long-term opioid use points to a diagnostic polysomnogram first.

Correct. Long-term opioid use is one of the settings where a polysomnogram, not an at-home kit, is used. Opioid medications are also a risk factor for central sleep apnea, which home kits cannot assess, since they assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders.

Home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders. Tell: her years of opioid use raise the possibility of central apnea and place her on the list of patients who need a polysomnogram instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

A questionnaire places a patient in a risk group and cannot diagnose; screening tools have value in symptomatic patients in high-risk settings such as preoperative evaluation. Tell: she already has symptoms, and opioid use decides which study she needs.

He has not yet had a chest radiograph, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests or a toxicology screen. What must happen before obesity hypoventilation syndrome can be diagnosed?
opts: About 90% of patients have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, but obese individuals are screened with or without it, and it is not one of the three criteria. Tell: the missing criterion is exclusion of other causes.
Confirm a body mass index above 35

The obesity criterion for this diagnosis is a body mass index above 30, and his 37 already meets it. Tell: 35 is the screening questionnaire's body mass index item; what he lacks is exclusion of other causes.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is first-line therapy, with weight loss, for the syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation, once it is diagnosed. Tell: his diagnosis is not yet established, because other causes have not been excluded.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion: obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake hypercapnia (arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg) must be joined by exclusion of alternative causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation. The workup includes a chest radiograph, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests and a toxicology screen.

opts: Correct. The overnight trigger is a lowest saturation under 80%, and 86% does not reach it. Tell: the awake trigger is 94% or less on room air, which is why an awake reading of 93% qualifies.
A serum bicarbonate in the normal range
A raised bicarbonate prompts screening, and above 27 it calls for an arterial blood gas. Tell: a value in the normal range is not a trigger; an awake saturation of 94% or less is.

Loud snoring and witnessed apneas are obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, which he already has, and about 90% of patients with the syndrome share them. Tell: screening is prompted by the added features, such as an awake saturation of 94% or less.

His awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 43 mm Hg (normal 35-45), and no other cause of hypoventilation has been found. How do his results measure against the criteria for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
opts: Met: obesity with snoring is enough

Snoring is an obstructive sleep apnea symptom found in about 90% of patients with the syndrome, but symptoms are not specific. Tell: the diagnosis turns on awake hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg, and his 43 falls short.
Met: his body mass index exceeds 35

The obesity criterion is a body mass index above 30, which his 39 meets, but obesity alone does not make the diagnosis. Tell: 35 is the screening questionnaire's body mass index item; what is missing here is a carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg.
Not met: body mass index is too low
His body mass index of 39 is above the cut-off of 30, so the obesity criterion is met. Tell: the criterion he misses is awake hypoventilation, since 43 mm Hg is not above 45.
Not met: carbon dioxide not above 45

Correct. The diagnosis needs all three: obesity (body mass index above 30), awake alveolar hypoventilation with an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, and exclusion of other causes. set2.q: A 61-year-old woman with a body mass index of 43 kg/m2, hypersomnolence and a raised serum bicarbonate is being evaluated for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Which test is the gold standard for her?
opts: Sleep study with oxygen saturation alone

Oxygen saturations feed the screening features, such as an overnight lowest saturation under 80%, but they do not measure carbon dioxide. Tell: the gold standard adds continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring to polysomnography.

A home kit assesses obstructive sleep apnea and is set aside when there is awake hypoventilation. Tell: the gold standard for this syndrome is polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.

An awake arterial blood gas shows the carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg that the criteria require, but it is a daytime measurement. Tell: the named gold standard is the overnight study with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring.
Sleep study with carbon dioxide monitoring

Correct. Polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring is the gold standard for obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Following carbon dioxide through the night captures the hypoventilation of the syndrome alongside the obstructive events that coexist in about 90% of patients.

opts: Correct. An oral appliance is not effective in patients who have no teeth (or in severe obstructive sleep apnea). He is edentulous, so the mouthpiece he asks about is the option to avoid, even though he cannot tolerate his mask.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated, which describes him. Tell: his lack of teeth limits the oral appliance, not this procedure.
A nasal expiratory resistance device uses his own breathing to produce expiratory positive airway pressure and does not depend on teeth. Tell: the option tied to having teeth is the oral appliance.

Positional therapy with a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps the patient on his side and fits events that occur when supine. Tell: missing teeth do not limit it; the oral appliance is the option that needs them.

opts: A split-night study records the first 2 hours to set severity, then switches to continuous positive airway pressure titration when obstructive sleep apnea is significant. Tell: her baseline disease is mild to moderate, which calls for the whole night of recording.

Patients may present in their 50s and 60s, so her age is typical, not a prognostic marker. Tell: the feature tied to poor prognosis is significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis.

opts: Correct. Central sleep apnea is treated by addressing the underlying cause first, and in heart failure the step is to optimize heart failure therapy. His worsening edema shows his heart failure is not controlled; continuous positive airway pressure is considered afterward, then adaptive servo-ventilation if it fails.

Adaptive servo-ventilation follows a failed trial of continuous positive airway pressure and carries safety concerns in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Tell: his first step is the cause, his poorly controlled heart failure.
Reducing opioids is the cause-directed step when opioid medications drive central apnea. Tell: he takes none; his cause is heart failure, so the step is optimizing its treatment.

set2.q: A 48-year-old man has loud, habitual snoring, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches and nocturia. His wife has seen him stop breathing and wake gasping. His blood pressure is poorly controlled on two medicines. His neck circumference is 18 inches, and his posterior oropharynx is crowded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness in the differential. Tell: it does not explain witnessed apneas, gasping awakenings and loud snoring, which are events of an airway obstructing during sleep.

Correct. Loud habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, awakening with gasping, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, nocturia and poorly controlled hypertension are its history findings, and a large neck and a crowded posterior oropharynx are its examination findings. Narrowing of the upper airway by soft tissue or structure causes it.

Central sleep apnea sounds very similar, with insomnia, frequent awakenings and daytime sleepiness, but snoring is less common and it clusters with heart failure, stroke, opioids or high altitude. Tell: loud habitual snoring and a crowded oropharynx point to an obstructed airway.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome needs obesity (body mass index above 30) plus awake hypoventilation, an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, with other causes excluded. Tell: nothing here shows awake hypercapnia; his findings are those of an airway that obstructs at night.

set2.q: A 55-year-old man is having a split-night polysomnogram. The first 2 hours of sleep show significant obstructive sleep apnea. What happens during the rest of the night?
opts: Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered for central sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure fails. Tell: his first 2 hours show obstructive apnea and nothing has failed yet; the second half titrates continuous pressure.

Recording the whole night untreated is the all-night polysomnogram, performed when baseline sleep-disordered breathing is mild to moderate. Tell: his first 2 hours already show significant disease, which switches the night to titration.

Correct. In a split-night polysomnogram the first 2 hours of sleep are recorded to determine severity, and if obstructive sleep apnea is significant, the rest of the night is a continuous positive airway pressure titration that finds the exact pressure needed to keep the airway open.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is the choice for obesity hypoventilation syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation. Tell: the split-night protocol titrates continuous positive airway pressure once significant obstructive apnea is seen.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure reports insomnia, frequent awakenings and nocturnal dyspnea. His wife says he rarely snores, and his breathing at night shows Cheyne-Stokes breathing (hyperventilation alternating with apnea). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome needs obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg with other causes excluded. Tell: nothing here shows obesity or awake hypercapnia; his pattern is the heart failure breathing of central apnea.

Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings in suspected sleep apnea. Tell: they do not explain a sleeping pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea in a patient with heart failure, the risk factor tied to central apnea.

Correct. Heart failure is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, especially through Cheyne-Stokes breathing, hyperventilation alternating with apnea from increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide and a prolonged circulation delay to the carotid chemoreceptors. Insomnia, awakenings and nocturnal dyspnea fit, and snoring is less common than in obstructive apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea brings loud, habitual snoring, and its airway collapses while the patient keeps trying to breathe. Tell: rare snoring with hyperventilation alternating with apnea in a man with heart failure points to a central cause, the brainstem signal failing.

set2.q: A 51-year-old woman with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has a fasting glucose of 118 mg/dL (normal 70-99) and triglycerides of 210 mg/dL (normal below 150). Which consequence of her sleep disorder do these results reflect?
opts: Hypothyroidism is a concomitant condition that raises the risk of obstructive sleep apnea, checked with thyroid-stimulating hormone when suspected; it is not a listed consequence. Tell: raised glucose and triglycerides are metabolic effects of the apnea itself.

Untreated obstructive sleep apnea increases cortisol; it does not cause a deficiency. Tell: the listed endocrine changes are increased C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid with decreased growth hormone and prolactin.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is 2 to 3 times more prevalent in obstructive sleep apnea, but it is a liver condition. Tell: high glucose and triglycerides point to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

Correct. Patients with obstructive sleep apnea have increased prevalence of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and diabetes complications, and the disease is independently associated with increased glucose and triglyceride levels. It may also worsen cardiovascular risk in metabolic syndrome.

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman snores loudly, feels tired during the day and is treated for high blood pressure. No one has seen her stop breathing. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and her neck (shirt collar) measures 15.5 inches. Using the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire, which result fits her?
opts: A score of 3 misses her age: she is 63, older than 50, so the A item is a yes. Tell: her four yes answers are snoring, tiredness, treated pressure and age, and the band stays intermediate either way.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 1 + observed 0 + treated pressure 1 + body mass index 34 (not above 35) 0 + age 63 (older than 50) 1 + neck 15.5 inches 0 + female 0 = 4, the intermediate band (3 to 4). She has 3 yes answers to the first 4 questions, but none of the add-ons (male, body mass index above 35, neck 16 inches) applies.

The add-on rules need 2 or more yes answers to the first 4 questions plus male gender, a body mass index above 35 or a 16-inch neck. Tell: she is female, her body mass index is 34 and her collar is 15.5 inches, so she stays in the 3-to-4 band.
A score of 5 counts her body mass index, but 34 kg/m2 is not more than 35. Tell: without the B item her total is 4, and her neck of 15.5 inches is also under the 16-inch item.

opts: The syndrome is awake hypoventilation in an obese individual, so hypercapnia without obesity does not define it. Tell: three criteria are needed, and her body mass index of 29 fails the obesity one.
Not met: carbon dioxide is too low
Her arterial carbon dioxide pressure of 50 mm Hg is above the cut-off of 45, so that criterion is met. Tell: the criterion she fails is obesity, with a body mass index of 29 not above 30.
Not met: body mass index not above 30

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires obesity (body mass index above 30), awake hypoventilation with an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, and exclusion of alternative causes. Her carbon dioxide of 50 qualifies, but a body mass index of 29 is not above 30, so the diagnosis cannot be made.
Awake hypercapnia is one criterion, and her 50 mm Hg meets it, but the diagnosis also needs obesity, a body mass index above 30. Tell: her 29 falls just short of the obesity criterion.

set2.q: A 55-year-old man with long-standing untreated obstructive sleep apnea has blood tests drawn. Which laboratory change is expected from his untreated disease?
opts: Prolactin decreases in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, along with growth hormone. Tell: of the listed endocrine effects, the increases are C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid.
Cortisol increases in untreated obstructive sleep apnea, alongside C-reactive protein and amyloid. Tell: the hormones that decrease are growth hormone and prolactin, not cortisol.

Correct. The endocrine effects of untreated obstructive sleep apnea include increased C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid, with decreased growth hormone and prolactin. Proinflammatory cytokines also rise, and they improve with continuous positive airway pressure.
Growth hormone falls in untreated obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: the markers that rise are C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid; growth hormone and prolactin are the two that drop.

set2.q: A 58-year-old man with loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness is seen for evaluation before elective surgery. He has never been tested for sleep apnea. Which property makes the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire suited to this visit?
opts: Severity is measured during a sleep study: a split-night polysomnogram records the first 2 hours of sleep to determine severity. Tell: the questionnaire gives a low, intermediate or high risk of having the disease, not a grade of disease he has.

Correct. The questionnaire has been used as a preoperative evaluation tool for people without a known diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea who may be at risk for perioperative complications, and it has the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires. A highly symptomatic patient in a high-risk setting is where it has value.

The questionnaire is singled out for the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires, the property that suits catching at-risk patients before surgery. Tell: its strength is not missing people at risk, which is sensitivity, not specificity.
It confirms the diagnosis before surgery

A questionnaire estimates risk; obstructive sleep apnea is confirmed on a polysomnogram, with 5 or more obstructive events per hour plus symptoms, or 15 or more. Tell: the score places him in a risk group and does not replace the sleep study.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated episodes, each 10 seconds or longer, of slowed, shallow, restricted breathing. Airflow is reduced but does not fall by 90%. How are these episodes classified?
opts: A mixed apnea has no airflow, with effort absent at first and resuming during the latter part of the event. Tell: his airflow is reduced, not absent, so there is no apnea here to classify as mixed.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing that occurs repeatedly during sleep in episodes of 10 seconds or longer. An apnea needs a fall in airflow of 90% or more for at least 10 seconds, which his episodes do not reach, so these are hypopneas.

An obstructive apnea is a fall in airflow of 90% or more for at least 10 seconds with continued respiratory effort. Tell: his airflow stays above that threshold, so the episodes are hypopneas whatever the effort channel shows.

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops signaling. Tell: he keeps breathing, slowly and shallowly, so neither airflow nor effort has stopped during these episodes.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 38-year-old long-haul truck driver has untreated obstructive sleep apnea with marked daytime sleepiness and is reluctant to start treatment. What should he be told about his rate of driving accidents compared with people without the disorder?
opts: 2 to 3 times is the higher prevalence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: the driving-accident figure is a single number, 2.5 times.

Correct. Untreated obstructive sleep apnea carries 2.5 times the rate of driving accidents, because daytime sleepiness increases motor vehicle crashes. For a man who drives for a living with marked sleepiness, that risk is a reason for counseling and treatment.
3 times is the risk of hypertension in untreated obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: driving accidents carry a separate figure, 2.5 times, driven by daytime sleepiness.
3 to 6 times is the risk of sudden cardiac death at night in untreated disease. Tell: the driving-accident figure is lower, 2.5 times, and comes from daytime sleepiness.

set2.q: A 59-year-old woman with a neuromuscular disease causing generalized weakness has snoring and morning headaches. Her awake room-air oxygen saturation is 92% (normal 95-100%). Which study should evaluate her for sleep-disordered breathing?
opts: At-home kits are set aside in neuromuscular weakness and in awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia. Tell: she has both, so a home kit is the wrong study even though her snoring and headaches suggest obstructive sleep apnea.
ruled out by a stated finding

Waiting leaves her symptoms and low awake saturation unexplained, while the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing rests on a sleep study. Tell: her weakness and hypoxemia call for a polysomnogram now.
A positive airway pressure titration is used when the diagnosis is already known, to set the device pressure. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet; her first study must be a diagnostic polysomnogram.

Correct. Neuromuscular weakness and awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia are both conditions in which a polysomnogram is used instead of an at-home kit. Her room-air saturation of 92% is below normal, and a polysomnogram can also find sleep disorders other than obstructive sleep apnea.

set2.q: A 62-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea uses continuous positive airway pressure nightly but still has daytime sleepiness. He also has coronary artery disease, cirrhosis and generalized anxiety disorder. Which treatment calls for caution because of his other conditions?
opts: Positional therapy with a sleep belt or shirt has no comorbidity caution attached and fits events that occur when supine. Tell: his heart, liver and psychiatric conditions are named cautions for the stimulants, not for positioning.
Diet and exercise for weight loss
Diet and exercise for weight loss is a risk modification for obstructive sleep apnea with no listed caution. Tell: his comorbidities raise concern for a stimulant drug, not for a lifestyle change.

Correct. Stimulants such as modafinil or armodafinil are used with caution in patients with cardiovascular, hepatic or psychiatric conditions, and he has all three: coronary artery disease, cirrhosis and an anxiety disorder. Nervousness and anxiety are also listed side effects.

Nasal steroids are used for nasal congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis, with no caution tied to heart, liver or psychiatric disease. Tell: the caution for those conditions is attached to the stimulants.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has trouble falling asleep and asks for a sleeping pill. Which option should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Use of alcohol or sedatives is a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the risk modification is to avoid alcohol and other sedatives. A sedative sleeping pill would add a risk factor to his untreated apnea.
Diet and exercise for weight loss
Diet and exercise for weight loss is a named risk modification for obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: it is advice to give him; the item on the avoid list is sedatives, along with alcohol.

Referral to a sleep physician, with proper counseling, is part of patient education for obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: this is part of his care, not something to avoid; sedatives are what he should stay away from.
Positional therapy with a sleep shirt

Positional therapy with a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps the patient on his side when events occur supine, a non-pharmacologic option. Tell: it carries no warning; sedatives and alcohol are the ones to avoid.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man had a stroke last year. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing during sleep, and a home sleep apnea kit has been ordered. What is the best next step?
opts: Proceed with the home kit as ordered

A home kit can serve uncomplicated suspected obstructive sleep apnea, but stroke is listed among the conditions that call for a polysomnogram. Tell: his stroke, not his snoring, decides the type of study.
ruled out by a stated finding

Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective treatment once obstructive sleep apnea is diagnosed. Tell: he has no diagnosis yet, and his stroke also raises the question of central apnea, so a polysomnogram comes first.

Stimulants such as modafinil treat sleepiness and need caution in cardiovascular conditions. Tell: no diagnosis has been made, and the decision in front of you is which sleep study to order after a stroke.
Change the order to a polysomnogram

Correct. Stroke is one of the conditions in which a polysomnogram is used instead of an at-home kit. Stroke is also a risk factor for central sleep apnea, and at-home testing assesses obstructive sleep apnea and is not sufficient for central apnea, so the order should change.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man who takes long-term opioid medications has central sleep apnea confirmed on polysomnography. He has no heart failure and lives at sea level. Which step treats the underlying cause?
opts: Optimizing heart failure therapy is the cause-directed step when heart failure drives central apnea. Tell: he has no heart failure; his listed cause is opioid medication.
ruled out by a stated finding

Stimulants such as modafinil are used for sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnea, with cautions and many drug interactions. Tell: a stimulant leaves the cause untouched; reducing opioids treats what is driving his central apnea.

Correct. Central sleep apnea is treated first by addressing the underlying cause, and when the patient takes opioid medications, the step is to reduce the opioids. After that, continuous positive airway pressure is considered, and adaptive servo-ventilation if it fails.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is the step after continuous positive airway pressure fails, not the opening move. Tell: the treatment sequence starts with the underlying cause, which for him is his opioid medication.

set2.q: A 44-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has respiratory events on polysomnogram that occur when he sleeps on his back and not when he lies on his side. He wants a measure to add to his care. Which therapy targets this pattern?
opts: Correct. Positional therapy fits when events occur in the supine position: a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps him lying on his side. His events are confined to back-sleeping, the exact pattern it addresses.
Nasal steroids treat nasal congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: he has no nasal symptoms; his events depend on his body position.

Palatal implants are for mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: nothing says he cannot tolerate pressure therapy, and his events are tied to position.

Tracheostomy is a cure because it bypasses the site of upper airway obstruction, but it is a surgical airway. Tell: his events depend on body position, which a sleep belt or shirt addresses without surgery.

set2.q: A 55-year-old man started continuous positive airway pressure for obstructive sleep apnea 2 months ago. A repeat polysomnogram on the device shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion. Which complication of his therapy has developed?
opts: Correct. Patients using continuous positive airway pressure are listed among those at risk for central sleep apnea. Repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion mean airflow stops because effort stops, the polysomnogram finding of central apnea.

Residual obstructive apneas would show continued respiratory effort, the chest and abdomen moving against a collapsed airway. Tell: absent thoracic-abdominal excursion means absent effort, which is the central pattern.
ruled out by a stated finding

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is awake hypoventilation, an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg in an obese patient with other causes excluded. Tell: his finding is a sleep event pattern of apneas without effort, not awake hypercapnia.

Sleep-related hypoventilation is the third category of sleep-disordered breathing and accompanies about 10% of obesity hypoventilation syndrome, with fewer witnessed apneas. Tell: his study shows repetitive apneas without effort, the central apnea pattern.

set2.q: A 50-year-old man has a polysomnogram as part of a research study. He has no sleepiness, fatigue or insomnia, and no one has noted snoring or pauses in his breathing. The study shows 7 predominantly obstructive events per hour. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Criteria for diagnosis are not met

Correct. Without symptoms, the diagnosis needs 15 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour; 5 or more counts only with a symptom such as sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia, choking or snoring noted by an observer. He has 7 events and no symptoms, so neither criterion is met.

7 events per hour would confirm obstructive sleep apnea only alongside a qualifying symptom. Tell: he has no sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia or observer-noted snoring, so the symptom-free threshold of 15 events per hour applies.

Central apnea shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion. Tell: his events are predominantly obstructive, and they fall below the diagnostic threshold for a symptom-free patient anyway.
Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective treatment once obstructive sleep apnea is diagnosed. Tell: his result meets neither diagnostic criterion, so there is no diagnosis to treat.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with obesity hypoventilation syndrome stopped her positive airway pressure therapy a year ago. She now has exertional dyspnea, an elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and pedal edema. Which complication has developed?
opts: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is tied to obstructive sleep apnea, but it does not raise the jugular venous pressure or cause pedal edema. Tell: hepatomegaly with those signs is right-sided heart failure.

Central sleep apnea is a sleep pattern of apneas without effort, with risk factors such as heart failure, opioids and altitude. Tell: her new findings are physical signs of right-sided heart failure, not a sleep event pattern.

Insulin resistance is a listed complication of the syndrome, but it does not produce edema or a raised jugular venous pressure. Tell: those signs, with hepatomegaly, point to right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome tends to progress if left untreated, and many patients develop cardiovascular complications, pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure. Elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and pedal edema are the listed signs of right-sided heart failure.

set2.q: A 34-year-old man on a mountain trek at high altitude wakes frequently at night. His tent partner notices that his breathing speeds up and then stops, over and over, without snoring. He has no heart failure and takes no medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Nocturnal asthma is on the differential for nighttime breathing complaints. Tell: the cycle of hyperventilation alternating with apnea, at high altitude, matches both the risk factor and the mechanism of central sleep apnea.

Correct. High altitude is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, in which increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide produces an unstable pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea. Frequent awakenings without snoring fit, since snoring is less common than in obstructive sleep apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea comes from upper airway narrowing and usually brings loud, habitual snoring. Tell: a repeating cycle of fast breathing and then no breathing, at altitude and without snoring, is the central pattern.

Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings. Tell: a repeating cycle of hyperventilation and apnea during sleep at high altitude is the breathing pattern of central apnea, not an anxiety episode.

set2.topic: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome: management and prognosis
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation syndrome: a. Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
set2.q: A 55-year-old man with a body mass index of 40 kg/m2 has obesity hypoventilation syndrome confirmed by exclusion. He has loud snoring, choking during sleep and resuscitative snorting, and polysomnography shows obstructive sleep apnea without sleep-related hypoventilation. Which first-line treatment fits him?
opts: Tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation is very effective but second line, kept for patients who fail or do not tolerate first-line therapy. Tell: he has not yet tried weight loss with positive airway pressure.

Medications are reserved for patients who fail diet and exercise measures, a second-line step. Tell: he has not yet tried first-line therapy, a weight loss program with continuous positive airway pressure.
Weight loss plus continuous positive airway pressure

Correct. First-line therapy for obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a weight loss program plus positive airway pressure, and when the syndrome coexists with obstructive sleep apnea, the device is continuous positive airway pressure. His snoring, choking and resuscitative snorting are the obstructive symptoms seen in about 90% of patients.
Weight loss plus bilevel positive airway pressure

Bilevel positive airway pressure is the device for obesity hypoventilation with sleep-related hypoventilation, the 10% subgroup with fewer witnessed apneas. Tell: his study shows obstructive sleep apnea without sleep hypoventilation, which pairs with continuous pressure.
